--- title: "Reproducible Research" description: "Chapter 17: reproducibility and credibility, Quarto documents with inline results, cross-references and citations, virtual environments, Shiny for Python dashboards, open science, and git." format: deck-html execute: echo: false freeze: auto --- # Reproducible Research A finding is credible only if it can be checked **Chapter 17** Polla Fattah --- ## By the end of today you can - explain why reproducibility is a matter of research integrity; - write a Quarto document with text, Python code, dynamic results, tables, figures, citations, and equations; - render it to HTML, Word, and PDF; - keep package versions with virtual environments and `requirements.txt`, and report them; - build a small Shiny for Python dashboard; - apply open science practices: sharing, protecting participants, preregistering, citing software. --- ## Three weeks before the deadline Twelve duplicated students are found in an early version of the survey export. They were removed in Chapter 3, but some tables were copied into the draft before that. Now every number copied by hand from Python into Word must be checked and replaced, one at a time. --- ## Reproducible and replicable | Term | Means | |---|---| | reproducible | same data and code give exactly the same results | | replicable | a new study with new data reaches the same conclusions | Reproducibility is the minimum standard: if results cannot be recomputed, asking whether they replicate is pointless. --- ## Most irreproducibility is everyday friction - a table copied before the data was corrected; - a spreadsheet cell edited by hand; - menu clicks nobody wrote down; - a package that changed its default. Habits from earlier chapters already guard against much of this. --- ## Habits you already have | Habit | Chapter | |---|---| | every step written as code in Python | 1 | | a dedicated project directory with relative paths | 1 | | raw data never edited by hand | 3 | | `np.random.seed()` before random steps | 7 | Today adds the last links: results placed into the report automatically, fixed software versions, and responsible sharing. --- ## Documents that contain their own analysis **Quarto** documents (`.qmd`) mix text and code. When **rendered**, the code runs and its numbers, tables, and figures are placed into a web page, Word document, PDF, slide show, or book. This course's book and these slides are written in Quarto. **Jupyter Notebooks** (`.ipynb`) are popular for exploration, but Quarto plain text is vastly cleaner for Git and reproducible reports. --- ## A complete Quarto document ````markdown --- title: "Three friends' sleep" format: html jupyter: python3 --- My three friends slept 6.3 hours on average last night. ```{{python}} import numpy as np sleep = [6.5, 7.0, 5.5] print(round(np.mean(sleep), 1)) ``` ```` --- ## The three parts | Part | Where | Holds | |---|---|---| | YAML header | between the `---` lines | title, author, output format, Python kernel | | Markdown text | the body | `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `# Heading`, `- ` bullets | | code chunks | between ````{python}```` and ```` ``` ```` | Python code run when rendering | In VS Code or Positron: click **Render** or run `quarto render report.qmd`. --- ## Inline code: numbers never typed by hand Inline expressions inside a sentence are evaluated and replaced by their result: > The sample included 600 graduate students from 5 faculties. If a student is added or removed, the sentence changes with the data. This is the permanent cure for the problem three weeks before the deadline. --- ## What happens when you render ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["report.qmd
text + code"] --> B["Jupyter runs
the Python code"] --> C["report.md
text + results"] --> D["Pandoc"] D --> E[HTML] D --> F[Word (.docx)] D --> G[PDF] ``` The code runs from the beginning every time. Anything created by hand in an interactive terminal makes rendering fail: a built-in reproducibility test. --- ## A results chapter in Quarto ````markdown --- title: "Chapter 4: Results" format: docx jupyter: python3 bibliography: references.bib execute: echo: false --- ```{{python}} #| label: setup #| message: false import pandas as pd import data2thesis as dt students = dt.students semesters = dt.semesters ``` The sample included 600 graduate students from 5 faculties. Table @tbl-faculty shows wellbeing by faculty, which declined as in earlier studies [@author2020]. ```` `format: docx` gives the Word file supervisors want; `echo: false` hides the code but keeps it in the `.qmd`. --- ## A numbered table from code ````markdown ```{{python}} #| label: tbl-faculty #| tbl-cap: "Wellbeing in the first semester, by faculty." merged = semesters[semesters['semester'] == 1].merge(students, on='student_id') summary = ( merged.groupby('faculty') .agg(Students=('student_id', 'count'), Mean=('wellbeing', 'mean'), SD=('wellbeing', 'std')) .reset_index().round(1) ) summary ``` ```` Chunk options start with `#|`. A `tbl-` or `fig-` label makes a numbered, cross-referenced item. --- ## What the reader sees > The sample included 600 graduate students from 5 faculties. Table 1 shows wellbeing by faculty. ::: {#4992efbe .cell results='asis' execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
Faculty Students Mean SD
0 Education 148 61.9 13.2
1 Health Sciences 154 59.0 11.6
2 Humanities 95 61.7 11.7
3 Natural Sciences 87 61.3 10.5
4 Social Sciences 116 58.9 12.1
``` ::: ::: --- ## References and citations ```bibtex @book{wickham2023, author = {Wickham, Hadley and Çetinkaya-Rundel, Mine and Grolemund, Garrett}, title = {R for Data Science}, publisher = {O'Reilly Media}, year = {2023} } ``` `[@wickham2023]` in the text becomes a formatted citation, and the reference list is added. Zotero, Mendeley, and EndNote export BibTeX. A `csl:` line switches between APA, Vancouver, Harvard, and thousands more. --- ## Equations ```markdown $$ \text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{stress} + \beta_2 \times \text{support} $$ ``` $$ \text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{stress} + \beta_2 \times \text{support} $$ LaTeX notation, between dollar signs. Renders identically in HTML, Word, and PDF. --- ## One line changes the output | Format | YAML | Notes | |---|---|---| | web page | `format: html` | interactive; for sharing online | | Word | `format: docx` | for comments; `reference-doc:` applies university styles | | PDF | `format: pdf` or `format: typst` | run `quarto install tinytex` or use fast Typst | | slides | `format: revealjs` | for presentations | A whole thesis can be a **Quarto book**, one `.qmd` per chapter. --- ## Parameterised reports ````markdown --- title: "Wellbeing report" format: html jupyter: python3 params: faculty: "Education" --- ```{{python}} faculty_data = semesters.merge(students, on='student_id') faculty_data = faculty_data[faculty_data['faculty'] == params['faculty']] ``` This report describes the students of the Faculty of Education. ```` ```bash quarto render faculty-report.qmd -P faculty:"Health Sciences" ``` One report, five deans, five versions. --- ## Packages change A default changes, or a function disappears, and an analysis that runs today may fail, or give different results, in two years. ```bash # 1. Create a virtual environment python -m venv .venv # 2. Freeze installed package versions pip freeze > requirements.txt # 3. Later or on another computer: restore exact versions pip install -r requirements.txt ``` `requirements.txt` lists every package and version. Share it with your code. --- ## Report software versions ```python import sys, statsmodels, sklearn, pandas print(f"Python: {sys.version.split()[0]}") print(f"pandas: {pandas.__version__}") print(f"statsmodels: {statsmodels.__version__}") ``` Name the versions of Python and key analysis packages in the thesis methods section. --- ## Shiny: let readers ask their own questions A report answers its author's questions. Readers want *"What about my faculty?"* | Idea | In Shiny for Python | |---|---| | inputs | `ui.input_select()`, `ui.input_radio_buttons()`, sliders | | outputs | `ui.output_plot()`, `ui.output_table()` | | user interface (`ui`) | where inputs and outputs appear (`ui.page_sidebar()`) | | server | Python code that computes outputs from inputs | --- ## Reactivity ```{mermaid} flowchart LR F["Input:
faculty"] --> S["@reactive.calc
selected() data"] S --> P["Output:
trend plot"] S --> T["Output:
summary table"] M["Input:
measure"] --> P M --> T ``` When an input changes, Shiny reruns only what depends on it. --- ## The dashboard: layout ```python from shiny import App, render, ui, reactive import pandas as pd app_ui = ui.page_sidebar( ui.sidebar( ui.input_select("faculty", "Faculty", choices=faculties), ui.input_radio_buttons("measure", "Measure", choices=measures) ), ui.card(ui.output_plot("trend")), ui.card(ui.output_table("summary")), title="Graduate Student Wellbeing" ) ``` --- ## The dashboard: server ```python def server(input, output, session): @reactive.calc def selected(): return wellbeing_data[wellbeing_data["faculty"] == input.faculty()] @render.plot def trend(): df = selected() meas = input.measure() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8)) sns.lineplot(data=df, x="semester", y=meas, hue="study_mode", ax=ax) return fig app = App(app_ui, server) ``` `@reactive.calc` refilters only when the faculty changes. --- ## What the dashboard draws ::: {#db22ac12 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='8' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](17-reproducible-research_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=747 height=324} ::: ::: Education, wellbeing. Host on shinyapps.io or Posit Connect; Shinylive runs Python apps entirely in the browser. --- ## Open science: sharing data and code | Include | Why | |---|---| | raw data, or how to obtain it | the starting point | | cleaning and analysis code | every step | | the Quarto source | the report itself | | `requirements.txt` / `uv.lock` | the software versions | | a codebook | what each variable means | OSF and Zenodo give a permanent **DOI**. A **licence** (CC BY for data, MIT for code) states what others may do. --- ## Removing names is not enough ::: {#1aaaf70e .cell results='asis' execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
faculty study_mode gender has_children n
7 Education Part-time Male Yes 3
15 Health Sciences Part-time Male Yes 3
21 Humanities Part-time Female Yes 3
5 Education Part-time Female Yes 4
``` ::: ::: Only 3 students are part-time male students with children in Education. In a small department, such a description points to recognisable individuals. --- ## Protecting participants - group categories or remove unneeded variables; - share summary data only; - follow the consent form: if it promised anonymised data, that is all; - when data cannot be shared, a **synthetic** dataset lets others run the code. --- ## The garden of forking paths ```python # Five defensible analyses of the exact same data: # 1. Standard t-test # 2. Outliers trimmed (|z| < 2) # 3. Log-scale t-test # 4. Mann-Whitney U rank test # 5. Linear model with covariate ``` No real group difference. Five defensible analyses, 1,000 simulated studies. --- ## Choosing afterwards inflates false positives | Analysis strategy | False positives | |---|---| | one planned analysis | ~5% | | best of five, chosen afterwards | ~11% | | best of ten, chosen afterwards | ~14% | No individual choice is wrong. The problem is choosing *after* seeing the result. --- ## Preregistration - record hypotheses, design, and planned analysis before seeing the data; - in a time-stamped registry: OSF Registries or AsPredicted; - confirmatory analyses follow the plan; exploratory ones are labelled as such; - a **registered report** is accepted before data collection, whatever the results. --- ## Citing software > *"Analyses were carried out in Python version 3.13 (Python Software Foundation), with data manipulation in pandas (McKinney, 2010), statistical tests in SciPy (Virtanen et al., 2020), and regression in statsmodels (Seabold & Perktold, 2010)."* Open-source package developers are researchers who depend on being cited. --- ## In your field: psychology and medicine In 2015, 100 psychology studies were repeated. | | Originals | Replications | |---|---|---| | significant results | 97% | 36% | | average effect size | full | about half | Small samples, flexible analyses, and selective publication. The response: preregistration, registered reports, and sharing. Medicine has required trial registration since 2005. --- ## Keeping a history with git (optional) | Term | Means | |---|---| | repository | a project folder whose history Git tracks | | commit | a saved snapshot with a descriptive message | | push | copy commits to GitHub, also a backup | | pull | bring down changes made elsewhere | Code editors (VS Code, Positron) have visual Git buttons. List private data in `.gitignore`. --- ## Practical lab: the Chapter 17 playground Work through the playground exercises in your browser, with hints and solutions. The Quarto and Shiny for Python exercises run from the downloadable project (`chapter17.zip`). --- ## Practical exercises 1–3: Quarto 1. Render the tiny document, change a value, and round with inline code. 2. Turn an earlier analysis into a report with a numbered table and figure. 3. Add references, cite them, and switch the citation style. --- ## Practical exercises 4–6: Shiny and open science 4. Add a slider for the semesters shown in the dashboard. 5. Which variable would you remove or group before sharing, and why? 6. Add a sixth analysis to `forking_paths()`: what happens to false positives? --- ## Try this yourself Take one results paragraph from your own thesis draft: - find every number typed by hand; - replace each with dynamic inline code; - give each table and figure a label and a cross-reference; - render to Word, change the data, and render again. --- ## Troubleshooting guide (Part 1) | Symptom | Likely cause | |---|---| | rendering fails, terminal works | code relies on an object made interactively | | a number in the text is out of date | typed by hand instead of dynamic code | | "Table ??" in the output | label lacks the `tbl-` prefix | | PDF will not render | LaTeX missing; `quarto install tinytex` or use `format: typst` | --- ## Troubleshooting guide (Part 2) | Symptom | Likely cause | |---|---| | different results on another computer | package versions differ; use `requirements.txt` | | a Shiny output never updates | it does not consume the reactive data | | shared data identifies people | small cells not protected | | a "significant" result after many tries | forking paths; preregister | --- ## Completion checklist - [ ] every number in the text comes from dynamic code; - [ ] tables and figures are labelled and cross-referenced; - [ ] the document renders from a clean session; - [ ] package versions are recorded in `requirements.txt` and reported; - [ ] software and libraries are cited; - [ ] shared data has no small identifying cells; - [ ] confirmatory analyses were planned in advance. --- ## Misconceptions to leave behind (Part 1) | Misconception | Better mental model | |---|---| | reproducibility means sharing code | every step, decision, and version | | copying a few numbers is harmless | the most common way a thesis drifts | --- ## Misconceptions to leave behind (Part 2) | Misconception | Better mental model | |---|---| | defensible choices give sound results | choosing afterwards inflates false positives | | removing names makes data anonymous | combinations can identify people | --- ## The chapter in one sentence > **Keep text, code, and results together so the whole report rebuilds from the raw data with one command, and share it in a way others can check and participants can trust.** --- ## Next: Chapter 18 The next chapter looks at AI and Natural Language Processing in research: - coding open-ended responses with AI; - inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa); - text embeddings and semantic similarity; - prompt engineering and LLMs as research assistants; - responsible AI disclosure in academic thesis work. --- ## Questions How many numbers in your current draft were typed by hand? What would it take to rebuild your results from the raw data tomorrow?
